[ASSISTANT_SAID] In digital signal processing, a chirp signal is a signal whose frequency changes over time.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The function we will create is called chirpTone, and it takes four inputs: the duration T in seconds, the initial frequency f1 in Hz, the final frequency f2 in Hz, and the sampling rate fs in samples per second.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The output of the function is a column vector output containing a chirp tone with the specified parameters.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] To generate the chirp tone, we first need to define the time vector t using the sampling rate fs.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] We can do this by dividing the duration T into fs equally spaced time intervals, or samples, using the sampling period ts=1/fs.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] This will give us a time vector t ranging from 0 to T with length(t) samples.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Next, we need to define the frequency vector f that grows linearly from f1 to f2 over the duration of the chirp tone.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] We can do this using the formula f = f1 + (f2-f1)/(length(t)-1) * (0:length(t)-1).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] This formula creates a frequency vector f with the same length as the time vector t, where the first element is f1 and the last element is f2, with the intermediate values growing linearly over time.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Finally, we can generate the chirp tone output by taking the sine of the product of 2πf(t) and t, where f(t) is the frequency vector we just defined.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] We can do this using the formula output = sin(2*pi*f.*t).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] To test our function, we can call it with the desired inputs and store the output in a variable x.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] For example, x = chirpTone(10,1000,2000,4000) generates a chirp tone with a duration of 10 seconds, starting at 1000 Hz and ending at 2000 Hz, sampled at 4000 samples per second.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] We can listen to the chirp tone using the soundsc function.
